nameStory: The 'tailed' long-jawed orbweaver gets its name from a distinctive projection or extension at the rear of its abdomen that resembles a tiny tail. Like other long-jawed orbweavers, it has impressively elongated jaws (called chelicerae) that extend forward from its head like pinchers. The 'orbweaver' part comes from the classic circular webs these spiders construct, though they often position themselves stretched out along plant stems rather than sitting in their webs.
description: The tailed long-jawed orbweaver is a slender, elongated spider that specializes in stretching itself along plant stems to avoid detection. Its body is typically brownish or yellowish with a streamlined shape that makes it look almost stick-like when at rest. These spiders are medium-sized orbweavers, with females being noticeably larger than males. They're part of the stretch spider family, known for their ability to extend their long legs forward and backward in a perfectly straight line.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly elongated and narrow abdomen with a small projection or 'tail' at the rear end that sets it apart from other stretch spiders

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Stretches out in a perfectly straight line along plant stems with front and back legs extended, making it nearly invisible against linear plant material

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a small, delicate orb web often positioned at an angle among vegetation, but frequently abandons it to hunt by stretching along stems

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent jaws extend forward from the head like tweezers, with small eyes arranged in two rows above them

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females reach about half an inch in body length, while males are considerably smaller and more delicate

habitat: Look for tailed long-jawed orbweavers in wetland edges, marshy areas, and along streams where tall grasses and sedges provide plenty of linear hiding spots. They prefer areas with dense herbaceous vegetation near water sources, where their stretch-and-hide hunting strategy works best. You'll most often spot them in cattail marshes, wet meadows, and the brushy borders of ponds and slow-moving waterways.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build webs and establish territories in emerging marsh vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible, actively hunting and reproducing in dense wetland growth.
seasonality.fall: Females lay egg sacs before dying off, while some individuals may remain active into early autumn in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as eggs or juveniles in protected locations within marsh vegetation and debris.

funFact: When threatened, this spider can stretch itself so perfectly straight and still along a plant stem that it becomes nearly impossible to detect, even when you're looking right at it – it's like nature's ultimate game of statue!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other stretch spiders in the same genus, but the small 'tail' projection on the abdomen is the giveaway feature. Remember: if it's stretching along a stem AND has a little tail, you've found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: This is considered quite rare in New England with only one documented observation, making any sighting potentially significant for local biodiversity records. It's much more common in warmer regions to the south and may represent the northern edge of its range in our area.
compareHints: Unlike the Common Stretch Spider which has a more uniform abdomen, the tailed long-jawed orbweaver has that distinctive rear projection. The Green Long-jawed Orbweaver is typically more colorful with greenish hues, while this species tends toward browns and yellows. The 'tail' feature makes it relatively easy to distinguish from all its stretch spider relatives once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tetragnatha relatives, the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out with its vivid green coloration, while the Common Stretch Spider tends to be more yellowish or brownish, and the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver has distinctive metallic silver markings.
Among New England's long-jawed orbweavers, the Common Stretch Spider is distinguished by its extreme elongation and distinctive straight-line defensive posture.
Among its stretch spider relatives, the Elongate Stilt Spider has the most extreme body elongation - much more stretched than the Common Stretch Spider or Green Long-jawed Orbweaver.
Unlike the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver that stays near water and has greenish coloring, versicolor prefers dry areas and shows yellow-orange tones.

Among the Tetragnatha genus in New England, the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out for its distinctive metallic silvery appearance, while the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver appears more yellow-green and the Common Stretch Spider tends to be brownish.
Compared to its relatives, the Straw-colored Stretch Spider is consistently paler than the bright green T.
